I've taken to rereading the Lord of the Rings and have recently read the Silmarillion. Many people theorize about what Tom Bombadil is, or who he is, and I would like to share my theory. Tom Bombadil is a lesser Ainur, or a Maiar; a spirit as old as time itself (Gandalf, Sauron, and Saruman are all Maiar as well). Here is a quote taken from The Fellowship of the Ring when Tom is telling stories to the four hobbits:

"When they caught his words again they found that he had now wandered into strange regions beyond their memory and beyond their waking thought, into times when the world was wider, and the seas flowed straight to the western Shore..."

The line "when the seas flowed straight to the western shore" refers to the first age, and part of the second age, when Arda was flat and the undying lands were on the same plain of existence as Middle Earth. For Tom to know so extensively about the ancient world means that he is extremely old. The book calls the atmosphere of Tom's house elf like in spirit, but not elven. This makes sense because much of the enlightenment of the elves can be attributed to their time in the undying lands, where all ainur have free reign to reside in. Tom even tells stories about the waking of the elves:

"Tom went singing out into ancient starlight, when only the Elf-sires were awake."

Ancient starlight is a reference to the time before the years of the sun in Middle Earth, when there was only starlight. Tom even recalls the waking of the elves. The only beings this old are Ainur. Unlike other Maiar though Tom is content to be the master of the Old Forest without controlling anything. The creatures of the Old Forest belong to themselves and he does not attempt to control the forest. For this reason I believe Tom is not affected by the ring's malice (not the same as not turning invisible). He is the only character in the books not motivated by a desire to control others.

Anyways that's my rant. If you have your own theory I'd love to hear it.

..."As a story, I think it is good that there should be a lot of things unexplained (especially if an explanation actually exists)

And even in a mythical Age there must be some enigmas, as there always are. Tom Bombadil is one (intentionally)." (The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, p. 174)
